item.title: ‘A Huge Paradox’: Nepal Region Hit by Flood Is Known for Development and Disasters
item.description:
The quiet mountain valley in northern Nepal seemed ready for reinvention. Trade routes and hydropower projects were expanding as diplomatic tensions eased. Tourism was surging back.

Then the floodwaters came.

On Wednesday, a devastating deluge killed more than 160 people in the valley, part of the Rasuwa district near Nepal’s border with Tibet. Hundreds more remain missing as rescuers struggle to navigate the devastation.

Scientists are still trying to determine what circumstances led to the surging waters on Wednesday, but natural disasters have repeatedly set the region back, even as it has undergone rapid development.

“This is a very vulnerable region,” said Galen Murton, a geographer at James Madison University who has studied Nepal’s infrastructure, referring to the area’s susceptibility for natural disasters. “It creates a huge paradox.”

Floods and landslides are common in northern Nepal during the summer’s monsoon season. Scientists say the area is becoming even more prone to natural disasters as climate change raises temperatures that compromise the region’s towering glaciers.

A deadly flood last year swept away the Friendship Bridge, a crucial trade and transportation link between Nepal and China. In 2015, an earthquake in the region killed nearly 9,000 people.

“People here have lived with risks for centuries,” said Austin Lord, an anthropologist and senior fellow at the Stimson Center in Washington who has studied natural disasters in Nepal. “But the risks are changing.”

Around 50,000 people live in the rural district, according to Nepal’s 2021 census, the latest available data. The Himalayan region is home to a large population of Tamang people, an ethnic minority in Nepal, Mr. Lord said.

Many others have moved to the region over the past decade as major development has picked up and Nepal has shifted away from its traditional reliance on India by pursuing more business with China, Mr. Murton said. Trade routes, border crossings into China and Chinese-backed hydropower projects have expanded. The area has also grown in importance as an entry point for Chinese electric vehicles imported into Nepal.

The result has been an “economic boom,” Mr. Lord said. “There are a lot of opportunities” that have attracted more people to the region, he added. But the risks are still great. The river valley is one of the country’s “most vulnerable corridors” to natural disasters, he said.

Nepal’s government has not yet released details about those killed in the flood, but it said the missing included local residents, border security workers and employees government agencies. Mr. Lord said the toll was also likely to include residents of small settlements near the river, laborers working in the border economy and truck drivers.

Around 400 foreign tourists were also missing, according to Nepali officials, many of them from India. Hundreds had been visiting Nepal on a Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a Himalayan peak across the border in Tibet that is revered as the spiritual home of the god Shiva.

Access to the area and other popular sites in the region resumed only in the past few years. Tourism had slowed to a trickle during the coronavirus pandemic and amid disputes between India and China over the border region.

It had recently picked up again.

item.title: Fears of a Second Flood Grow as Rescue Efforts Continue in Nepal
item.description:
As emergency workers searched Himalayan valleys on Thursday for survivors of a colossal flood that killed hundreds of people, the Nepali and Chinese authorities warned that a second flood might be coming — with rescuers most at risk, according to an expert.

The landslide that set off Wednesday’s flood clogged the river system and created a barrier lake close to the border between Nepal and the Tibet region of China, the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources said Thursday evening. It said that rain forecast to fall over the next three days could more than double the lake’s water volume to over 176 million cubic feet, the equivalent of about 2,000 Olympic-size swimming pools.

The risk that the new lake could breach its rocky barrier and wreak havoc downstream was “high,” the ministry said, potentially causing areas such as the Gyirong border crossing, which had already been decimated by floodwaters, to be “struck by disaster again.”

The lake had already started to overflow on Thursday, forcing rescue efforts in Tibet to stop and sending water at speeds of more than 120 miles per hour into the same river that flooded a day earlier, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Friday morning.

Nepal’s disaster management agency on Thursday urged people to move away from riverbanks because of the risk of a second flood.

Another deluge would track the same path as the first, posing the most risk to people on search-and-rescue missions, said Austin Lord, an anthropologist and senior fellow at the Stimson Center in Washington, who has studied natural disasters in Nepal.

A second flood would be another challenge for rescue and assistance efforts already forced to navigate destroyed infrastructure and damaged communication lines. “Warnings of potential renewed floods are complicating an already challenging operation,” said David Fisher, head of delegation for International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Nepal.

While the flood would most likely be smaller and significantly less deadly, Mr. Lord said, the volume of water in the new lake is “not insignificant.” He compared its potential impact to that of a flood that hit the same area last year, killing at least eight people, destroying a key border bridge and disrupting trade between Nepal and China.

“We have no way of knowing how the dynamics would play out,” Mr. Lord said. “The area is so freshly volatile.”

But governments, residents and rescuers would have a crucial advantage this time: a heads-up.

“They’re running models of potential floods and visually monitoring the growth,” said Alton C. Byers, a senior research associate at the Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research at the University of Colorado, Boulder. “They can warn people.”

The Himalayas are dotted with thousands of glacial lakes, posing a constant flood risk if large, falling debris crashes into them. The region is known for being prone to natural disasters.

Scientists have said the deadly flood on Wednesday was probably caused by a massive rock landslide colliding with a glacier falling from the high mountains.

Mr. Lord said scientists were also monitoring what seems to be yet another new body of water forming at the initial impact point below the north face of Langtang Lirung, a mountain in Nepal near the border with China.

“It seems to have created a glacial lake that’s growing in size,” Mr. Lord said. “It may overtop or breach at some point in the coming days.”

Lily Kuo and Mujib Mashal contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Harald V, Norway’s King as Tradition and Modernity Collided, Dies at 89
item.description:
King Harald V of Norway, whose 35-year reign opened an ancient monarchy to a contentious cast of family connections, including a draper’s daughter; a celebrity shaman; and Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier, died on Friday. He was 89.

The king died at University Hospital Rikshospitalet in Oslo, the Royal Court said in a statement. He had been receiving treatment for a bacterial infection of his blood and members of the royal family had gathered at the hospital on Thursday as his condition deteriorated.

The king was born into a centuries-old lineage that shared part of its heritage with the British monarchy, anchoring him in a network of inherited privilege in an era when Europe was moving toward replacing all-powerful rulers with more ceremonial constitutional monarchs like Harald. He was a distant cousin of King Charles III of Britain.

Of his reign’s many collisions between tradition and modernity, perhaps the most perilous came recently.

This year, the United States Department of Justice released a huge trove of documents related to Mr. Epstein, including emails linking Crown Princess Mette-Marit, the king’s daughter-in-law, to the sex offender.

In the emails, the relationship between the crown princess and Mr. Epstein — unfolding several years after Mr. Epstein was convicted in 2008 on charges of soliciting a minor for prostitution — came across as intimate and teasing, and showed that she was closer to him than the palace had previously acknowledged. The disclosures prompted questioning of Mette-Marit’s suitability as a future queen and emboldened some Norwegians to call for the abolition of the monarchy.

There had already been some public questioning in 2001, when Crown Prince Haakon, the heir to the throne, married Mette-Marit Tjessem Hoiby, a former waitress, divorcée and single mother. But Harald himself had already begun the process of change that brought so-called commoners — people with no royal ancestors — into the regal House of Glücksburg created by his forebears. Risking a rift with his father, King Olav V, and threatening not to wed at all if his plans were frustrated, Harald had in 1968 married Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a clothing merchant and an undergraduate at the University of Oslo when they met.

Their secret on-again-off-again courtship lasted for nine years before Olav dropped his opposition and consented to their wedding.

The marriage was the start of a family tradition: Both of their children followed Harald’s example by choosing commoners as spouses.

The disclosures this year about Mette-Marit’s friendship with Mr. Epstein forced her to issue a statement saying that she regretted “having had any contact with Epstein.” But the royal family refused to comment further, opening it to accusations of evasiveness and more. “Can Mette-Marit become queen after this?” a leading newspaper editor asked.

The scandal was all the more incendiary because it emerged just days before Mette-Marit’s son, Marius Borg Hoiby, the stepson of Crown Prince Haakon, went on trial on multiple charges of rape as well as other crimes. In June, he was found guilty of many of the charges and sentenced to four years in prison, and has been under house arrest as he appeals the verdict. Also in June, the crown princess, who was diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis in 2018, underwent a successful lung transplant.

The crisis this year eclipsed other moments when Harald’s family had inspired public scrutiny. In 2002, his daughter, Princess Martha Louise, married an author, Ari Behn; they divorced in 2017, and he died by suicide in 2019. In 2022, the princess announced her engagement to Durek Verrett, an American and a self-proclaimed shaman who counted Gwyneth Paltrow among his celebrity clients and friends. They married in 2024.

Their relationship brought hostile attention to some of Mr. Verrett’s past utterances, including his claim that he had used an amulet — which he sold for $222 on his website — to combat Covid-19, and his assertion that cancer is a choice. The princess had also been criticized for many years for claiming to be clairvoyant and for urging others to contact “the angels and the divine universe.”

Disapproval of their relationship inspired media comparisons to the turmoil in the British royal family provoked by Prince Harry’s 2018 marriage to Meghan Markle. There were indeed parallels: In 2022, the Norwegian royal family announced that, like Prince Harry and his wife, Martha Louise and her partner would step back from royal duties; and, like Harry and Meghan, the princess and Mr. Verrett, who is Black, ascribed public criticism of their bond to racism.

But unlike the acrimonious rift in Britain between King Charles III and Harry, his younger son, Martha Louise characterized her separation from the royal family as friendly. For the Norwegian king’s part, he said that he and Mr. Verrett “agree to disagree.”

Harald was born on Feb. 21, 1937, on the royal Skaugum estate outside Oslo, the third child — after Princess Ragnhild and Princess Astrid — of Princess Martha of Sweden and the future King Olav V of Norway, who ruled from 1957 until his death in 1991.

Harald and Queen Sonja had two children, Martha Louise, born in 1971, and Haakon, in 1973. He is survived by them, his wife and six grandchildren.

The king’s early years were shaped by World War II, which began in September 1939. Six months later, German troops invaded Norway and the royal family fled. Harald’s grandfather, King Haakon VII — who had refused to surrender to the Germans — and his father, then called Prince Olav, took up residence in London, where a Norwegian government in exile had been established to oppose the German-backed administration of Vidkun Quisling, a Nazi collaborator who was in office for much of the occupation.

Along with his mother and sisters, Harald traveled to Washington, where he spent most of the war and where the family befriended President Franklin D. Roosevelt. At 7, he stood behind the president at his fourth inauguration in January 1945.

After the end of the war later that year, the royal family returned to Norway. Harald attended the University of Oslo, the Norwegian Military Academy (from which he graduated in 1959) and the University of Oxford in Britain, where he studied history, economics and politics at Balliol College in the early 1960s. He was known as an athlete, and as a yachtsman he was part of the Norwegian team at three Summer Olympics from 1964 to 1972, in Tokyo, Mexico City and Munich.

He became Norway’s king following the death of his father on Jan. 17, 1991, a new reign that was credited with greater openness toward the public than his predecessors had allowed. Beyond his acceptance of commoners into the royal family, he ordered the renovation of royal buildings, including the Royal Palace in Oslo, so that they could be opened to the public.

Harald was the country’s first Norwegian-born monarch since the 14th century. (After long political unions with Denmark and Sweden, Norway became independent in 1905.) Like other European monarchs, his powers as head of state were circumscribed by the Constitution and parliamentary convention to ensure that his political role was limited and largely formal. Much of his reign was underpinned by an economic boom that brought prosperity to Norwegians from offshore oil and gas deposits.

But in July 2011, he faced a brutal challenge to the nation’s self-image and self-esteem when Anders Behring Breivik, a far-right extremist, killed 77 people in attacks on government buildings in Oslo and on the island of Utoya. Some Norwegians compared the shock to the trauma of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks in the United States.

With an address to Norwegians, meetings with bereaved families and a public display of grief when he wept at a national memorial service, Harald was credited with emerging as a symbol of patriotic resolve and unity.

“Now it’s important that we stand together and support each other, and that we don’t let fear take over,” he told his compatriots on the night of the attacks.

In a rare interview with The New York Times a few months later, the king said: “I’ve always had the feeling that in times of crisis, that’s what we’re here for, really. That showed in 1940, and we’ll see if this will come out the same way. You do what comes natural to you, and if that’s correct, all the better for that.”

Lynsey Chutel and Henrik Pryser Libell contributed reporting.

item.title: Tips for Traveling While Pregnant
item.description:
When I was 20 weeks pregnant with my daughter, I took a babymoon with my now-husband. Though it was March, we encountered a 90-degree heat wave in Palm Springs, Calif. Still, I decided to hike in the desert in Joshua Tree National Park.

Barely 30 minutes in, I became overheated and my feet swelled up. Miserable, I called it off and retreated to our hotel.

It can often be hard to anticipate how traveling — even in less extreme conditions — could affect a pregnancy. Thankfully, doing some research and simple prep, and getting advice from your doctor can make things go smoother.

At least four to six weeks beforehand, describe your trip to your doctor so they can do a risk assessment to help determine if you're cleared for travel, said Dr. Mark Turrentine, a professor at the Baylor College of Medicine and a member of a panel that reviews pregnancy and travel guidelines published by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.

The ideal time to travel is between 14 and 28 weeks for most low-risk, singleton pregnancies, he said, adding emergencies are more common during the first 12 weeks or the early third trimester.

“You can get turned away from the airline at any point in pregnancy,” said Dr. Jennifer Doorey, an assistant professor in the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. She suggested always carrying a doctor’s letter that includes your due date and says you’re cleared to fly.

After 28 weeks, many international airlines require such documentation. After 36 weeks, some airlines won’t allow you on board except under special circumstances. The cutoff can be earlier for certain risk factors. Cruise companies often won’t allow pregnant passengers aboard after 23 weeks. Check with your carrier.

For your return, leave some wiggle room for possible delays.

Your doctor can help you assess available care at your destination and create a backup plan. An island or remote area may not have a hospital, a labor and delivery unit, or a neonatal intensive care unit.

“If your water broke and you got stuck in that hospital, would that be acceptable to you?” Dr. Doorey said.

If you’re taking a cruise, investigate the level of care on board and in ports. When flying, consider how long you’ll be in the air and over large bodies of water, and in what areas the plane could make an emergency landing, along with available medical options.

Check for travel advice from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization for areas at risk for mosquito-transmitted illnesses that can cause pregnancy complications and, with certain infections, birth defects. Protect yourself by wearing long-sleeved clothing, using pregnancy-safe repellents and sleeping inside with air conditioning and closed windows, Dr. Turrentine suggested.

Most U.S. health insurance plans don’t cover care abroad so contact your provider. Consider a separate travel medical insurance policy for emergencies and evacuation. While routine pregnancy care and childbirth are rarely covered, some emergencies are, so seek clarity.

Carry prenatal medical records in digital and hard copy. Bring an extra supply of prescription medications.

Stay hydrated. Dr. Doorey suggested drinking a bottle of water before the flight, finishing another on board and guzzling more if the trip is long.

Use compression socks to improve blood flow, reduce swelling and help prevent blood clots, including deep vein thrombosis. Walk around the plane at least every few hours.

Wear your seatbelt correctly. “You want it in the crease below the bump, like touching your two hip bones on either side,” Dr. Doorey said. Avoid elevating your legs on a car’s dashboard in case the airbag deploys, she added.

Book accommodations with air conditioning and an elevator, or ask for a low floor. Tell the staff you’re pregnant.

Consider splurging on a room with a view, said Alison Mullis, who runs a family travel blog. While visiting the Azores during her second trimester, she was sidelined by sickness, but said the vista she could see remained memorable.

Don’t pack too much into one day. Avoid hot tubs and monitor your body temperature — overheating is common, and especially risky, during the first trimester. Symptoms include heavy sweating, headache, or dark urine, among others. Drink cool water slowly and rest, Dr. Turrentine said.

Stay away from physical activities that could cause abdominal trauma, like skiing or scuba diving.

Be aware of urgent maternal warning signs, or symptoms associated with high blood pressure or preterm labor, Dr. Turrentine said. He advised seeking medical care for abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, contractions, a persistent headache and dizziness, among others. If you’re unsure, err on the side of caution.

Once you’ve been cleared by your doctor, traveling while pregnant is generally considered safe. Still, it can also be stressful. Using short-term anxiety medication is generally not advisable but speak with your doctor. Stretching, paced breathing, muscle relaxation exercises, splashing water on your face or redirecting your thoughts can help.

item.title: Canada Hires 48 Scholars Away From Top U.S. Universities
item.description:
Twenty-one universities in Canada announced on Thursday the hiring of dozens of researchers to join their top academic ranks, poaching the majority of the recruits from the United States.

Of the incoming 64 researchers, 48 will leave American campuses including Harvard, Yale and M.I.T., and the remainder are from Europe, Asia and Australia.

Turmoil in American academia, precipitated by a crackdown on prestigious universities by the Trump administration and attacks on scientific research groups, has allowed Canada a rare opportunity to lure some of those schools’ top minds north.

Their hiring is paid for through a Canadian government investment of more than 500 million Canadian dollars (about $364 million) in research fields that are strategically important, from global warming to artificial intelligence. The program was announced last December as part of a broader $1.2 billion investment in Canadian innovation projects, with a second round of 63 academics to be hired next year.

While scientists often shy away from political discourse, some are saying the Trump administration’s assault on science is behind their departure.

“I used to live in the country that I thought was the most enthusiastic about the prospects for science improving the human condition, of any country in the world,” said Phillip Zamore, the chair of RNA Therapeutics Institute at the University of Massachusetts. “And I woke up one day and that wasn’t true anymore.”

He has been recruited to McGill University in Montreal, which has also hired five other researchers, and will join the medical faculty.

“If scientists don’t stand up for truth, no one will,” Dr. Zamore said.

The Canada-bound brain drain from U.S. institutions began last year as the Trump administration put forward policies that targeted foreign students, academic freedom and funding for equity-related programs.

Kevin Hall, a nutrition scientist who left the U.S. National Institutes of Health last year, accusing federal officials of censoring his research on ultraprocessed foods, has been hired at the University of Ottawa.

“While certain countries are cutting research and turning their back on academic freedom, we’re doubling down on science,” Mélanie Joly, Canada’s industry minister, told reporters at the announcement, in Vancouver, of the new university hiring. She billed it as the world’s “largest talent attraction” project. The European Union has made a similar push.

“Years from now, we will look back at today’s announcement, and we will be able to seize the lasting impact of our choices,” Ms. Joly said.

Unpredictable decisions about funding prompted Seth Guikema, a professor in civil and environmental engineering, who has specialized in natural hazards modeling at the University of Michigan, to look elsewhere. His work focuses on how climate hazards inequitably affect communities, and that work has become harder to fund, he said.

“Every country sets its priorities in terms of what is going to get funded, and I think Canada has done a very good job of supporting research in areas that really matter to society,” said Dr. Guikema, who will start at Western University in London, Ontario in January.

The University of Toronto has also recruited six academics, including Sara Seager, a Canadian astrophysicist from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Universities in Canada are the latest pathway for some Americans to leave the United States, citing the Trump administration’s policies. Canada has also expanded citizenship eligibility for people who can prove their Canadian ancestry, resulting in thousands of applications from Americans.

item.title: Pro-Palestinian Activists Accused of Vandalizing Trump Resort Face Terrorism Accusation
item.description:
Scottish prosecutors will attempt to prove that pro-Palestinian activists accused of vandalizing one of President Trump’s Scottish golf resorts last year committed acts connected to terrorism. The move is the latest in a broadening effort in Britain to target protest groups with terrorism laws.

In March 2025, prosecutors say, seven members of the British protest group Palestine Action broke into the resort, Trump Turnberry. They dug up the turf and damaged the sprinklers. They sprayed the clubhouse with red paint. And they emblazoned “Gaza is not 4 sale” on part of the picturesque course.

All seven were charged with malicious damage to property and are set to face a judge in a preliminary hearing in Glasgow on Monday.

But the prosecutors’ 16-page indictment also argues that the vandalism was “aggravated by reason of having a terrorist connection,” which could lead to a harsher sentence if the accused were convicted.

In a social media post soon after the activists were arrested last year, Mr. Trump described them as “the terrorists who attacked the beautiful Turnberry” and said that “they did serious damage, and will hopefully be treated harshly.”

At the time, Palestine Action had claimed credit for carrying out several acts of vandalism, mostly against British sites connected to an Israeli weapons manufacturer, Elbit Systems. Three months after the Turnberry episode, the group said two of its members had vandalized planes at a British military base to protest what it described as Britain’s military support for Israel. The group posted footage of the episode online.

Days later, Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government announced it would ban Palestine Action as a terrorist organization, a contentious move that prompted fierce debate over free speech and the right to protest.

The ban was the first time Britain had used antiterrorism powers against a group for “serious damage to property” rather than because of the use or threat of violence against people.

Legal experts said the indictment against the protesters draws on 25-year-old laws originally designed to severely stiffen sentences for people convicted of murder or other serious crimes in the course of a terror attack.

Prosecutors in Britain have begun aiming to apply the same provisions to political protesters, with varying degrees of success. In one case, four Palestine Action activists convicted of vandalizing a building owned by Elbit in Filton, England, were sentenced as terrorists. In another case, however, a judge rejected prosecutors’s efforts to apply a terrorism connection to Palestine Action protesters accused of breaking windows at a Barclays Bank branch.

Huda Ammori, the co-founder of Palestine Action, accused prosecutors of trying to advance the agendas of Mr. Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of Israel, by pushing to sentence protesters as if they were terrorists.

“By hitting the profits of arms companies and by daring to spray paint on the golf course owned by the demagogue who has enabled Netanyahu’s crimes, we made powerful enemies,” she said in a statement. “The British government chose to appease them by criminalizing us as ‘terrorists.’”

That designation led to the arrests of several thousand protesters for holding signs that said: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.” The terrorism law used against Palestine Action criminalizes the wearing, display or publication of anything that expresses support for a banned group.

On Wednesday, the Trump administration also designated Palestine Action as a terrorist organization as part of what it called “Action Against Violent Far-Left Terrorist Networks,” saying in a statement that the decision “complements the U.K.’s proscription.”

Jonathan Hall, an independent adviser to the British government on terrorism laws, said the authorities were right to want more tools to prevent terrorism, which is broadly defined in British law and can include serious damage to property. But he said the government was grappling with when to apply those legal tools.

“The really tricky thing,” he said, “and I’ve got no brilliant answer for this, is where do you draw the line?”

Amnesty International has accused the British government of overreach. In the case of the vandalism at Turnberry, Felix Jakens, director of communications at the human rights organization, said that it was “completely disproportionate to equate painting on a golf course with terrorism.”

“A terrorism sentence stays with you for life,” he added, “and it’s shocking that the defendants could face such severe punishments for this nonviolent protest.”

While in office, Mr. Starmer rejected charges that his government was endangering free speech by targeting protesters.

In May, he said that he wanted “tougher action” taken toward protesters who chant certain slogans like “globalize the intifada” that cause fear among British Jews. The Metropolitan Police in London previously announced that they would arrest protesters for using the phrase.

Andy Burnham, who replaced Mr. Starmer as prime minister, has not directly confronted the issue since taking office last month. Some members of his Labour Party have made clear that they believe he should take a stand against the overuse of terrorism laws.

In February, judges at England’s High Court ruled that the government’s ban of Palestine Action had been unlawful, saying it was disproportionate and breached the right to protest. But he Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in June. The Supreme Court will consider the case in November.

item.title: You Can Photograph This Pretty Irish Castle. You Just Can’t Go In.
item.description:
The tourists come by the busload, disgorging from motorized behemoths that seem improbable for many Irish roads. With cellphones at the ready, they head for the photogenic Dunguaire Castle, a majestic 16th-century bastion rising beside a swan-favored corner of Galway Bay.

Overlooking the sea-scented village of Kinvara, Dunguaire (pronounced doon-GWEER-ah) could well be Ireland’s most photographed castle, its image in countless brochures and promotions. But a sign on the entrance gate suggests that Ireland, known as the land of 100,000 welcomes, might have to reduce that number by at least one: “CASTLE & GROUNDS CLOSED TO THE PUBLIC.”

There to say hello instead one recent morning was Fran O’Reilly, a retired researcher wearing a broad-brimmed hat as protection from the day’s Irish rarity of sustained sunshine. In her hand was a document featuring a QR code that, when scanned, opened to a prewritten email of disappointment, already addressed to various government officials, to which visitors could add their own words of dismay.

With the zeal of a seasoned campaigner, Ms. O’Reilly approached clutches of puzzled tourists to explain that not long ago, the castle was open for tours and banquets — until, she said, government officials got in their own way.

“About three years ago, they had a fight about money, and instead of sorting it out, they closed the gate,” she told a family from France. “So people like you, thousands of people every week, come from around the world to see this castle, and can’t.”

One of the French tourists scanned the QR code to join an effort that, at last count, had convinced 2,400 people from more than 50 countries to send missives of disenchantment to the powers that be. A quick perusal showed notes from a tour operator in Denmark, a study-abroad program director in the United States and many, many disgruntled Irish people.

“This place is one of the reasons that tourists come here, and what do they find: Ireland is closed,” one wrote.

When asked about the status of Dunguaire, the Shannon Airport Group, the government entity that owns the castle and closed the site in 2023, forwarded a brief statement that said, in part: “Relevant parties are actively exploring options for the future ownership and stewardship of the site with a view to securing its long-term protection and conservation. As these discussions remain ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage.”

For Ms. O’Reilly, member of a grass-roots group called Save Kinvara Castle, the statement was as vaporous as the exhaust fumes of the idling buses near the tower. “So this petition is a way of trying to say, ‘Enough,’” she said. “‘Get on with it.’”

The castle’s name translates as “fort of Guaire,” a seventh-century king. Technically a tower house, the structure was built around 1510 by the ruling O’Hynes clan as a defensive lookout and residence, but transformed over time into a symbol of permanence as integral to Kinvara’s identity as the sea.

From the outdoor seating at establishments along the quay — Connolly’s pub, perhaps, or the Pier Head restaurant — visitors can sit and, glass in hand, consider how the 75-foot tower has been a stone-silent witness to the evolving Irish story.

It was there, defining the horizon, as a place with a few crude buildings developed into the busy port of Kinvara. As the potatoes were harvested, the seaweed collected and the main street bustled on market days. As tenant farmers chafed under British landlords. As famine struck.

The mid-19th century calamity known as the Great Hunger devastated Kinvara with evictions, emigration and death. In a cow field a short walk from the castle, a modest monument marking the mass graves of hundreds features a prayer in Irish that translates as “May they all have a bed in Heaven.”

A diminished Kinvara took generations to recover, but life continued. In the castle’s shadows, people watered their horses, repaired the red sails of their single-masted Galway hookers and gossiped in forever-pubs like Green’s, where the weight of whiskey still sags the shelves. Some fought in the war of independence early in the 20th century, even tearing down the British police barracks on the main road, then endured the civil war that followed.

After the author and poet Oliver St. John Gogarty took possession of the castle in the 1920s, the building became a gathering place for the literary lights of the Celtic Revival. Then, in the 1960s, the building came into the hands of Lady Ampthill, who had once rocked British society with a divorce centering on an unconsummated marriage and a “virgin birth.”

John Conneely, a retired teacher steeped in local history, recalled seeing her ladyship riding sidesaddle in the fields and driving into the village with her two hounds beside her. Ever aware of her elevated station — she once referred to local residents as “natives” — Lady Ampthill is nevertheless credited with completing a restoration of Dunguaire before selling the castle in the early 1970s to a government entity overseeing regional tourism, a forerunner of the Shannon Airport Group.

“Otherwise, the castle would have fallen down,” Mr. Conneely said.

Dunguaire looked on as ancient pubs closed and chic cafes opened, as the local hotel became a refuge for asylum seekers, as the annual boat festival brightened the bay with red sails. As Granny Brogan kept watch from her candy shop window, and as a white-bearded German fisherman, Rainer Krause, rowed out from the pier every morning, for decades, in search of mackerel.

For most of the last half-century, Dunguaire was open to the public, offering tours, lectures and medieval banquets. It became an obligatory stop for visitors touring the West Coast of Ireland, a way station between the city of Galway and the Cliffs of Moher.

Several years ago, the Shannon Group, later rebranded as the Shannon Airport Group, worked out deals to transfer ownership of various tourist sites under its aegis to local authorities. Clare County Council took over Bunratty Castle. Limerick County Council took over King John’s Castle. But a similar plan to have Galway County Council acquire Dunguaire became mired in a bureaucratic bog, and the castle was closed.

So began years of structural assessments, financial projections and back-and-forth discussions, all rooted in Galway County Council’s refusal to take ownership without significant government funding for a nearly $6 million restoration.

Michael Owens, director of services for Galway County Council, said in an email that while the council did not have the “financial capacity” to reopen the landmark, officials recognized the castle’s historical value and “potential to serve as a critical tourism driver.” He also said that the national Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage was now “exploring the acquiring of title.”

But the talks have yet to open Dunguaire’s doors, leaving the Galway county councilor Geraldine Donohue to imagine the deterioration being caused by the lack of proper maintenance.

“Here we are, going all over the world promoting Ireland and how wonderful we are,” Ms. Donohue said. “And yet we can’t get together five million to open one of the most iconic, most photographed castles in the world.”

“We’re not asking you to build the castle,” she said. “It’s built!”

Outside Dunguaire, members of Save Kinvara Castle continued their campaign to shame the government into action. At his station near the locked gate, Eamonn Coy, a retiree, worked the economics angle, saying that tourism was essential to Kinvara, which has just 800 residents.

“The idea that we turn our backs on that is utter stupidity,” Mr. Coy said of the potential earnings.

Ms. O’Reilly greeted tourists disembarking from buses and cars in the dusty parking lot. She emphasized the lost opportunity — the missed chance to step back in time — to a pair of Canadian tourists who agreed that a banquet at the castle might have been worth staying the night.

The Canadian visitors walked up to the soaring monument of Ireland’s past, vacant now, save for the ghosts. On the other side of the padlocked gate, overgrown grass lapped against a portal that once led to souvenirs and the 16th century.

Then, like so many before them, they returned to their vehicle and headed on to the more welcoming Cliffs of Moher.

item.title: ‘The Sauna Is Hot and Uncomfortable’: Vote on E.U. Talks Makes Iceland Sweat
item.description:
Gudlaug Bjornsdottir had warned her family. If the talk over the dinner table turned to Iceland’s coming referendum on opening talks to join the European Union, she would get up and leave.

Polls show a starkly divided country heading into the vote on Saturday. Many people have strong opinions about whether Iceland should maintain its hard-won independence or seek the stability and protections that would come with E.U. membership.

So perhaps inevitably, despite Ms. Bjornsdottir’s admonitions, the dinner conversation in the tiny town of Talknafjordur one recent Friday eventually landed on the referendum. “I am leaving, like it or not,” Ms. Bjornsdottir stood and said, a wine glass still in her hand.

Her family promised not to mention it again, and she returned to her seat.

This exchange, in Iceland’s remote northwest, encapsulated an unusually heated debate in this proudly agreeable nation over what could be a watershed moment for its 400,000 people. If the vote passes, the country will start a yearslong process of E.U. accession negotiations. A second referendum, on whether to actually join the bloc, would be held once a deal was reached.

Many Icelanders have spent months wrestling with how to speak with each other about the divisive choice.

“It has become something of a ‘hot potato,’” Arni Ingolfsson, a 55-year-old program manager at a tech company, wrote in an email. He said he was avoiding talking to his co-workers and even a close relative about the issue.

“It’s bombarding everyone, from every angle — everywhere,” said Lisa Margret Gunnarsdottir, 31, an advocate for Icelandic students. She said that there were extreme disagreements in her immediate family and that no one talked about anything else.

“The sauna is hot and uncomfortable these days,” said Greta Gudjonsdottir, 57, who works in tourism. She said she had not yet decided how she would vote but just wanted the whole thing over with.

With this vote, Icelanders are trying to figure out the best way forward in an increasingly precarious and divided world. For years, they had little reason to doubt that their country would remain safe, stable and sovereign. Then NATO, to which Iceland has long entrusted its security, threatened to crack under pressure from President Trump, while wars, climate change and tariffs shook the global economy.

Some “yes” voters say that Iceland should seek strength in numbers — and the financial stability of being part of one of the world’s biggest economic blocs — by moving toward joining the E.U.

Many opponents worry that membership in the bloc would cost Iceland its autonomy on several fronts. Icelanders are acutely aware that their country only gained full independence in 1944, after centuries of Norwegian and Danish rule.

Fishing is widely seen as the biggest concern about E.U. membership, with many “no” voters worrying that joining the bloc could hurt this major industry.

“It feels very existential, this debate,” said Eirikur Bergmann, a politics professor at Bifrost University in Iceland. “It’s really a fight over where Iceland belongs.”

Of course, Iceland has had contentious times before.

The 2008 global financial crisis hit the country particularly hard — its banks collapsed, and its currency plummeted. The strife led Iceland to explore E.U. membership, but that effort fizzled after its economy started to recover.

Still, many Icelanders live with the memory of that economic precarity, which is animating the referendum debate both for sides. Some think joining the European economic bloc could help lower Iceland’s high inflation and interest rates, while others worry that it could burden the country with regulations that make it less nimble.

Ms. Bjornsdottir and her husband, Thor Magnusson, who were having the recent family dinner in Talknafjordur, make their living off fish. He goes out alone on a boat. They work together to prepare the catch and sell the fish out of a glass house, which runs on the honor system.

Like other Icelandic fishermen, they believe that staying out of the E.U. will give them more control over their own fate.

The discourse over the referendum has become so heated that Margret Einarsdottir, a law professor at Reykjavik University, said she saw echoes of American-style polarization and misinformation in some of the ugliest corners of the domestic debate.

“I’m sad about how much anger is in this discussion,” she said. Icelanders do not shy away from disagreement. But this feels different, she and other experts said.

“We are not used to it,” Dr. Einarsdottir said.

Others see things more positively, saying it is a good thing that Icelanders can disagree openly but cordially, and still keep their tight communal bonds.

“It’s a lively debate, which is also a very healthy sign of democracy,” said Bjarni Mar Magnusson, a partner at a law firm, Polestar, and a former dean of the law faculty at Bifrost University.

Hallgrimur Oddsson, the founder of Evropustraumar, an Icelandic think tank focused on relations with the E.U., said that despite the acrimony, Icelanders still share the same values.

“At the end of the day,” he added, “we can still talk to our neighbor.”

item.title: Who Is Norway’s New King?
item.description:
After the death of King Harald V on Friday, Norway has a new king.

Crown Prince Haakon, 53, will succeed his father. While the role of king in Norway has become mostly a ceremonial and symbolic position, the monarchy still plays a public role in Norwegian society, representing the country at home and abroad.

As heir to the throne, Haakon has spent a life carrying out royal duties, and he increasingly took on a more central role as his father’s health deteriorated.

Haakon was born in Oslo on July 20, 1973, to Harald and Queen Sonja. He has an older sister, Princess Martha Louise. After attending public and private schools in Oslo, he followed family tradition and enrolled in the Norwegian Armed Forces.

After graduating from the Royal Norwegian Naval Academy, Haakon bucked the tradition of enrolling at Oxford University in England, like his father and grandfather had, and studied political science at the University of California, Berkeley. He then went to the London School of Economics, where he graduated in 2003 with a master’s degree in development studies, with a focus on international trade and African studies.

Like his father, he wedded a “commoner” — a person with no royal ancestor — but his 2001 marriage to Mette-Marit Tjessem Hoiby was not without controversy. She was divorced and had a young child from her first marriage, and the tabloids soon dug up details of her party-girl past. But the family stood by the couple, and Mette-Marit was accepted by the public.

In recent years however, revelations over her friendship with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein soured public perception. Her eldest son, Marius Borg Hoiby, has also had run-ins with the law. In June this year, an Oslo court convicted Mr. Hoiby of rape, domestic violence and other charges, and sentenced him to four years in prison.

Princess Mette-Marit underwent a lung transplant this year.

Haakon and Mette-Marit have two children together, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus.

Although Haakon has an older sister, Norway’s succession law dictated that the heir must be male. That law changed in 1990, and Haakon’s eldest daughter, Ingrid Alexandra, is the next in line to the throne.

item.title: Six Months In, Iran’s Regime Stands, U.S. Goals Remain Unmet
item.description:
It was supposed to be quick.

Still, six months after the U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran, the conflict drags on. The Trump administration has replaced its military war with an economic one, but the result is likely to be no different, analysts said, with a lack of American clarity about goals, a decline in American credibility and a strategic defeat.

One thing remains constant, however. The ordinary people of Iran are bearing the brunt of the war, victims of both the United States and their own leaders.

On the first day of the war, Feb. 28, President Trump promised Iranians that “the hour of your freedom is at hand.” Six months later, his administration is trying to impoverish them further, hoping against hope that they will revolt against a repressive, militarized regime and overthrow it.

The Iranian leadership, increasingly dominated by military men, sees its own survival as the nation’s, and it considers the sacrifices of ordinary Iranians as a necessary act of patriotism and even martyrdom. It has been ever more ruthless in stamping out the slightest signs of dissent.

It is hard to dress up what has clearly been an American failure to bend Iran to its will, despite the might of the combined American and Israeli militaries. Not only has the Islamic Republic survived, but it effectively controls the Strait of Hormuz. It has strengthened its influence in the region, with even the countries it was bombing a few months ago trying to reinvigorate ties with Iran.

“The war has failed to deliver U.S. objectives,” said Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa program at Chatham House.

Suzanne Maloney, an Iran expert and head of foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, judged the war a failure. “We did a lot of damage to Iran, but they have come out stronger than before,” she said. Iran’s neighbors have decided they must find a modus operandi with an Islamic Republic that is not going away.

American credibility among allies has suffered along with Mr. Trump’s own reputation for avoiding costly, interminable wars in the Middle East and promoting “affordability” at home. And it has made his promise to liberate ordinary Iranians look hollow.

“This war has really overtaken the Trump presidency,” Ms. Maloney said.

“Operation Epic Fury” began with a joint American-Israeli surprise attack on Iran, which killed the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and many of his officials, while badly wounding his son and now successor, Mojtaba.

Weeks of intense bombing destroyed much of Iran’s air force and navy and badly damaged its missile program. But the population did not rise up and the leadership did not fracture.

Iran’s military restored many of its missile launchers and attacked key American allies in the region as well as American bases, which were inadequately defended. It effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz and caused global economic disruption.

Several thousand Iranians, including children, have died — the numbers are hard to verify — and 18 American service members.

The original “Operation Epic Fury” has been replaced with what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced as “Operation Economic Outcast,” designed to isolate Iran further and crash its badly damaged economy.

“This is a sustained campaign to collapse every last option for Iran,” Mr. Bessent said. “The campaign we begin today will gather force with every day that follows, and it will not end until this regime stands alone.”

Despite rhetorical flourishes about D-Day and the fall of the Berlin Wall, Mr. Bessent did not indicate how long this economic war will last, what instruments it will use or what it aims to achieve.

Is the American goal once again the collapse of the regime? Or to force the opening of the Strait of Hormuz? Or to bring a more desperate Iran back to the negotiating table to reach a sustainable settlement of both the strait and Iran’s nuclear program?

“There is no clear articulation of America’s goals,” said Esfandyar Batmanghelidj of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, a research organization based in London. “But if you don’t define behavior change, sanctions as coercion fail.”

Iran, already the target of many thousands of sanctions, is considered unlikely to surrender because of a few more. More likely, analysts said, is that the country will respond in time by escalating its attacks on ships in the Persian Gulf and on American allies, which could produce another round of American bombing.

Washington is betting it can achieve through intensified economic strangulation what six months of war could not, said Sina Toossi of the Center for International Policy, a Washington think-tank.

Washington is trying to do that by demanding international compliance even as its relations with much of the world grow more coercive and transactional, with more countries choosing to ignore Mr. Trump’s dictates.

“The capacity to hurt Iran is clear,” Mr. Toossi said. “The path from pain to capitulation or collapse is not.”

With American objectives unclear, the confusion is real in Tehran, too, said Ali Vaez, the Iran project director for the International Crisis Group. They will wonder, he said: “Does the U.S. want to achieve collapse, capitulation or compromise?”

Given that Iran’s leaders see the effort to strangle them as another form of warfare, Mr. Vaez said, the new American strategy has two risks. If it fails, the only option left is to return to military escalation. And if it works, it may lead Iran to escalate to break the U.S. naval blockade.

“In either case, it won’t produce what the administration seems to want, which is to use sanctions as an alternative to war,” he said. “It’s more likely to be a prelude to another round of military warfare.”

Iran’s public-facing leadership, including President Masoud Pezeshkian and Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the parliamentary speaker, has been blunt about the economic imperatives to ending the war. They have warned of the consequences of hungry people and economic collapse.

They nonetheless take a consistent line on negotiating with Washington, insisting on a return at minimum to the June Memorandum of Understanding, which Mr. Trump signed but now says is “over.” They also continue to negotiate with Oman about managing the strait in a way Washington is unlikely to accept.

But no matter how much Iran concedes, there is a widespread mistrust that Mr. Trump will deliver on economic benefits and sanction relief. Despite the dire economy, the leadership appears united on retaining control of the strait.

The supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, is seen as closer to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps and less risk-averse than his father.

Some wonder if Mojtaba is even alive; he has not been seen in public and the last communiqué from his office was on Aug. 9.

For the moment, the situation is relatively static, a sort of phony war, with neither side firing at each other and relatively loose blockades of the strait in both directions, allowing some oil to escape.

The new strategy of enhanced economic strangulation has the benefit of being gradual and hard to monitor, lowering the temperature on the conflict, which may help Mr. Trump and the Republicans in the run-up to November’s midterm elections, while promising that victory, really, is just around the corner.

But the stalemate is also risky, said Ellie Geranmayeh, an Iran expert with the European Council on Foreign Relations. “There is an increasing view in the White House that you can’t deal with this Islamic Republic,” she said. “It’s a dangerous moment, with both Tehran and D.C. concluding that no deal is possible with the other.”

Jeremy Shapiro, a former State Department official now at the European Council on Foreign Relations, remains puzzled why Mr. Trump has not taken any of the available offramps to ending an enormously unpopular war at home. By pushing even more economic sanctions, he said, Trump officials “are pretending they’re still fighting instead of pretending that they’ve won” — or admitting that they’ve lost.

As ever, Iran’s leadership won’t pay the cost, Mr. Shapiro said, it will be its people that do.

item.title: ‘Better to Kill Us’: Fear Over Malaysia’s Plan to Send Back Myanmar Migrants
item.description:
Two years ago, Muhiduzamal fled religious persecution and civil war in his native Myanmar, traversing land and sea for four months before arriving in Malaysia. As at home, he found work in a paddy field, and moved into a traditional Malay home, a wooden structure on stilts.

He tried to register as a refugee with a United Nations agency in Malaysia, and was waiting for an appointment. But without that status, Malaysia considered Mr. Muhiduzamal, 35, who is a Rohingya Muslim and uses only one name, to be in the country illegally. In June, he was arrested and sent to a detention center, his brother said.

Malaysia has more than 10,000 undocumented migrants from Myanmar in custody. Last month, it announced plans to send about half of them back home. The migrants, their families and rights groups say that they are worried that once the migrants are back in Myanmar, the military government there will conscript them — men and women — and force them into battle. Rohingya fear the worst: They are stateless in their own country and have suffered what the United Nations and the United States have determined was a genocide conducted by the Myanmar military.

“It is better to kill us in Malaysia rather than send us back to Myanmar,” said Mohammad, 25, who has refugee status and lives in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia’s capital, but asked to be identified only by part of his name while discussing his brother’s case.

“My brother will be killed if he is sent back, as the junta in Myanmar will send him to the frontline to fight.”

Over the past decade, hundreds of thousands of people from Myanmar have sought refuge in Malaysia in the hope of escaping ethnic cleansing and a brutal junta. Tens of thousands have refugee status in Malaysia but they still face intensifying discrimination. Hundreds of undocumented migrants have died in detention.

In a statement released on Thursday, Malaysia’s Home Ministry said that the influx of migrants had become a “major financial burden, caused serious social problems and created a real security threat to the country.” It added that about 1,500 migrants in detention centers would be “voluntarily repatriated” next month, using a Myanmar Navy fleet of two warships and a hospital ship.

“There is no clarity on what the government means by voluntarily,” said Ramachelvam Manimuthu, the president of the National Human Rights Society, a prominent nonprofit in Malaysia. “Was it a free and informed choice? Does voluntary deportation also mean detainees were given a choice of being registered as refugees?”

Fear and panic is rippling through the Myanmar migrant community.

“Everyone is on alert,” said Bibi, an undocumented 18-year-old Rohingya woman who has lived in Malaysia for over a year and asked to be identified only by part of her name. “We are scared of the authorities and the public.”

Yap Lay Sheng, of Fortify Rights, a nonprofit, said, “People are skipping work even when it means losing daily income and keeping their children from refugee schools because they fear being targeted by the public and authorities.”

Malaysia does not grant political asylum to migrants. But if they are given refugee status by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees — even after arriving illegally — Malaysia allows them to stay.

Now Malaysia is starting its own registration system for refugees. On Thursday, the Home Ministry said that over 4,000 detainees, primarily Rohingya, will be subject to this program. Migrant advocates say the registration process must provide every person with a fair, individualized assessment of their protection needs, including access to interpreters, legal assistance, and a right of appeal.

“The government must expedite the refugee registration, and make sure that refugee cardholders have lawful access to work, education, housing, and guarantee against the arbitrary arrests, detention and pushbacks,” Mr. Yap said.

Fahmi Fadzil, Malaysia’s communications minister and the government spokesman, has said that migrants would not be deported if their lives are threatened in Myanmar, saying that the authorities had been assessing who could be returned and under what conditions.

About five years ago, soon after the coup that brought the military to power in Myanmar, Malaysia said it repatriated over a thousand migrants. It is unclear how they fared.

“For people who fled Myanmar seeking safety, forced return represents a profound betrayal of the protection they sought abroad,” said Nickey Diamond, who is originally from Myanmar and on Fortify Rights’ board.

Hla Maung Thein, 32, an undocumented ethnic Chin migrant from Myanmar, was arrested this month and is being held at a detention center in Kuala Lumpur, according to his wife. She added that sending him back to Myanmar, even if he got home to his native Rakhine state, would amount to a death sentence.

“I have heard that people who were previously sent back by ship never made it home,” said Nwe Nwe, his wife, who also asked to be identified by part of her name. “Even if my husband makes it home, he will certainly be forced to serve military service in the Arakan Army,” she said, referring to the rebel group that controls most of the state.

The U.N. refugee agency has said that conditions in Myanmar are not safe for migrants to return.

Mr. Manimuthu of the National Human Rights Society said the Malaysian government should put a hold on the deportations until there is an international consensus that it is safe for detainees to return.

“History has shown we cannot accept the words of Myanmar authorities,” he added. “The repatriation of refugees cannot be based on hope and prayer. It must be solid evidence that it is safe for returning.”

item.title: Inside Afghanistan’s Secret Schools for Girls
item.description:
Ayesha goes to a secret school six days a week, mainly to keep seeing people outside her home. It’s the only way to avoid total isolation under Taliban rule, she says. It’s the only way to feel alive.

“Without that connection,” she said, “I don’t know what would happen to me.”

Now 18, Ayesha once dreamed of studying psychology at university. The Taliban ended that dream when they banned formal education for girls beyond sixth grade in 2022.

But Ayesha has been defying the Taliban’s rules for years, sitting in a classroom hidden behind the corridors of a primary school. Thousands of such programs operate across the country under the Taliban’s radar.

Clandestine schools were once seen as a stopgap, a way for girls to keep up with their education until the Taliban were gone. But five years after the Taliban’s return to power, nearly 2.5 million Afghan girls have been locked out of secondary school.

They can go to religious schools or study at home with private instruction. But across the country, girls are risking arrest by going to school in secret. Others fail sixth grade on purpose, to remain in their classrooms for as long as possible.

Principals, teachers and parents operate the schools through a clandestine effort, fighting for what they fear may be a lost cause: to save a generation of girls from ignorance. The Taliban’s leaders do not appear willing to rescind the ban, even while some local officials tolerate the secret schools, worried about denying their own daughters an education.

In interviews with more than 50 students, educators, therapists and parents, many said they feared the ban would do permanent damage — to girls and to Afghanistan’s social fabric. All asked to be identified only by their first names, for fear of retaliation.

Even girls who finish their education have few prospects; the Taliban have banned women from most jobs, and opportunities to go abroad are scarce. Reports of suicidal thoughts, self-harm and rates of underage marriage are on the rise, according to teachers and humanitarian organizations.

Nevertheless, some girls refuse to give up their fight for an education.

“We are also part of this society,” Ayesha said. “Just let us be who we want to be.”

Late one night recently, Ayesha received a text from her friend Zuhal, 17, who said she would not be coming to class the next day. Zuhal’s father had beaten her, saying that there was no point in attending an underground school.

Ayesha recalls crying as she read Zuhal’s message. She has become known among her friends as the one they can confide in, the apprentice therapist. She said she prayed in her bedroom and urged Zuhal to come back. “If you sit at home, it’s finished for you,” Ayesha told her. “Nobody else is going to do anything for you.”

Zuhal returned to school a few days later but said she would be able to come only when her father is away.

Ayesha’s secret classroom is concealed inside an official primary school. The playground is filled with the shouts of younger students, and hundreds of tiny, colorful shoes are lined up at the entrance to the building. But beyond their classrooms, a door leads to a hidden passageway tucked behind a corner, which leads to the secret classroom for older girls.

To avoid detection, the students vary their routes to the school and avoid walking in groups. Still, now and then, the Taliban burst into the school unannounced, as they did one morning in July during Ayesha’s midyear physics exams. The principal locked the students inside, and 14 young women kept scribbling in silence.

The classroom remains undiscovered. On one occasion, when the girls were not at school, the Taliban tore down the artwork on the walls in a common room near the classroom, Ayesha recalled.

There used to be a time, students and a teacher explained, when a Taliban inspection would send them fleeing through the back door, or rushing to the basement where they would lock themselves in the dark and shush those who cried.

As the students moved up to Grade 12, Taliban visits don’t frighten them as much anymore. Many said they feel contempt for the group.

“Are they expecting the country to develop by depriving half of the population of education?” said Palwasha, one of Ayesha’s classmates. “We don’t want anything other than the basic rights Islam gave us.”

Only a tiny fraction of girls in Afghanistan can receive a secondary education through secret schools; even fewer, like Ayesha and Palwasha, study an international curriculum and speak English fluently. Palwasha wants to launch her own clothing brand. Ayesha knows she won’t be able to study psychology at a university in Afghanistan when she graduates, so she counsels her classmates.

This is the extent of Ayesha’s social life, and it will vanish in a few months. There is no secret school after Grade 12.

“Girls, you are here now,” Ayesha recalled their teacher saying as they sat down for their midyear exam. “But at this time next year, you will be at home.”

The Taliban have taken credit for one measure of success in education: Primary school enrollment for girls rose from 78 percent in 2021 to 87 percent in 2024, according to UNESCO and UNICEF. That’s mainly because day-to-day security has improved across Afghanistan since the war ended with the U.S. withdrawal in 2021. Schools that had been closed reopened, and crossing a street to reach a classroom no longer presents a daily danger.

But the overall picture is alarming. Nine out of 10 Afghan children age 10 cannot read an age-appropriate piece of writing, according to UNESCO. Only one in four Afghan women is literate. Girls who want to continue their education sometimes face additional obstacles from their families.

Laila, 21, joined a secret school to study computer science and languages two years ago, more than 500 miles from her home in one of Afghanistan’s most conservative provinces. She said she threatened to kill herself if her family did not let her attend.

On a recent morning, she worked on computer science and Duolingo lessons in a clandestine Grade 11 classroom. In the school’s darkened corridors, students walked silently past colorful presentations on the human body and the solar system. Dozens more studied in the basement library.

Laila and hundreds of other girls take in-person classes by day and online by night with volunteer tutors around the world, from the United States to the Netherlands to Hong Kong, most of them high school students in a global network of peer-to-peer support.

Even two years after enrolling, Laila faces surprise visits from her younger brother, who tells her she has dishonored the family by being “so free.” Her father is more open-minded but fears gossip if a relative or neighbor finds out, Laila said.

Laila now speaks four languages fluently, including English, and is learning Korean. If she can leave the country after graduation, she said she will study graphic design in Canada or South Korea.

“I want to share these opportunities with other girls from my province, but I can’t,” Laila said.

During their first rule, between 1996 and 2001, the Taliban banned both primary and secondary education for girls, arguing that secular schools were contrary to their hard-line vision of Islam. They said it was a temporary measure, until they could establish a more compatible education system, but they never did.

After coming back to power in 2021, they made similar claims about the public school system that expanded during the 20-year U.S. occupation, and still maintain that the ban is temporary.

“We hope that one day girls’ schools will reopen,” the Taliban’s spokesman, Zabiullah Mujahid, said in an interview earlier this year. “This situation also deeply affects many officials of the Islamic Emirate who have daughters,” he added, referring to the name the Taliban have given to Afghanistan.

But five years into their second rule, the temporary ban once again appears permanent.

The ban comes directly from Kandahar, the group’s seat of power in the south and home to its secretive leader, Sheikh Haibatullah Akhundzada. Many Taliban officials privately say it should be lifted, but no one challenges their leader’s order.

In practice, many Taliban turn a blind eye to schools operating in secret. The principal at one secret school, where some girls pay fees if their families are able, said he had enrolled the sons of Taliban intelligence officers for free to maintain a cordial relationship.

They know Laila’s school well: Taliban police and intelligence officers visit weekly to ensure that female students wear their hijabs correctly and don’t mix with boys, who attend the same school legally.

But they can order the school shut at any time. All schools in Afghanistan, even religious schools, which are permitted for older girls, face an array of rules and frequent, sometimes surprise, inspections.

When they see the Taliban approach, the guards at Laila’s school warn the teachers and the principal by walkie-talkies and then sound a distinctive bell to alert the students.

Najib, the school principal, said that when he asked some unfamiliar Taliban officers to show him their ID on a recent visit, one shouted, “My ID is my gun.”

“And my gun is my pen,” Najib said he replied. He cited Quranic verses about the imperative to educate all children, and that seemed to satisfy them.

The Taliban left.

Many younger Afghan girls try to delay as long as possible what Ayesha and Laila are going through.

In December, Somaya, 12, took her sixth-grade final exams but skipped the tests in Dari language, social studies and Quran studies, hoping to fail and repeat her final year.

“I love going to school,” she said. “I simply wanted to stay.”

Weeks later, Somaya’s teacher told her she could come back. There was only room for her in Grade 4, so she sometimes helps teach since she already knows the curriculum.

Fatima, 12, a student at another school, tore up her final sixth-grade tests last year, hoping that her teachers would fail her and let her repeat the grade. But they passed Fatima anyway, she said.

As Fatima spoke softly in her family’s living room in Kabul, her father, Azizullah, wept and left the room.

“I cry when I think about how often she says she wants to be a doctor, and how now it’s all over,” Azizullah said.

But Fatima bounced back. Weeks later, she passed an entrance exam for an underground school.

Tasnim, a primary schoolteacher, said she leaves the farewell parties for her Grade 6 students because she can’t bear seeing them cry. She no longer has an answer when they ask her, “What was this all for?”

When her own daughter, Kowsar, completed sixth grade, Tasnim convinced a colleague to take her into her class so she could repeat by taking the spot of an absent student.

Her daughter’s graduation certificate reads “Successfully promoted to Grade 7.”

“We try to make them happy,” Tasnim said. “But there’s no Grade 7.”

The restrictions on women and girls are the primary reason the world has shunned the Taliban, but they have promoted religious schools, or madrassas, as an alternative. The girls in those schools must wear black coverings from head to toe, and they are allowed to study science and English as well as religious subjects.

Zala, a sixth-grade student, plans to enroll in a religious school after leaving primary school. “At least we still have an opportunity to keep studying,” she said.

Other students say the madrassas are a poor substitute. Classes deemed less important than religious ones — physics, chemistry and mathematics — are merged into one. And girls are not permitted to use the more advanced curriculum for boys.

“These subjects are pushing us ideologically toward the Taliban,” said Zahida, 17, about Islamic studies, religious history and discussions about politics and jihad led by teachers who embrace the Taliban’s hard-line views.

Ezat, Ayesha’s principal, recently turned the school where her classroom is hidden into a madrassa to ease pressure from the Taliban. He said he hopes teachers can keep providing what he described as a “modern education.”

To what extent and for how long, he does not know.

After the Taliban formalized their ban on education in 2022, many teachers were left without jobs. They kept teaching for free, or for smaller salaries at schools that remained open, or in underground classes across the country.

Many say they feel disillusioned.

At a recent staff meeting, employees in a secret school in Kabul talked about how to keep motivating students. “But who is motivating us?” Kamela, one of the teachers, remembered thinking.

“I see the Taliban in my dreams,” she said. “They’re running after us, beating us and closing the school.”

Safiullah Padshah contributed reporting.
